text: Every single night, you close your eyes and slip into a private cinema.
Worlds appear, people return, impossible things feel completely real.
And when you wake, most of it dissolves like breath on glass.
But here is the question almost nobody stops to ask:
Where do dreams actually come from?
For most of history, we answered with magic.
Messages from the gods, visits from spirits, prophecy in disguise.
But the real answer is stranger, and more intimate.
Dreams are not sent to you from anywhere. They are generated by your own brain, while you sleep.
The engine room is a sleep stage called REM.
Down in the brainstem, neurons fire off random bursts of electrical activity, with no input from the outside world.
Your body is paralysed, your eyes dart around, and your brain sparks with self-made noise.
Now here is the clever part. Your cortex, the storyteller of the brain, cannot tolerate random noise.
So it reaches into that chaos and starts weaving it into something coherent.
A character, a place, a plot. It spins meaningless sparks into a narrative.
And what does it weave with? Your own raw material.
Fragments of memory, faces you know, places you have been, emotion left over from the day.
That is why dreams feel so personal. The brain stitches yesterday's leftovers into tonight's story.
This does not happen just once. Across a night you cycle through sleep stages roughly every ninety minutes.
And REM periods get longer toward morning.
That is why your most vivid, elaborate dreams arrive in the last hours before waking.
Scientists call one version of this activation-synthesis.
The brainstem activates the cortex with random signals, and the cortex synthesises the best story it can.
On this view, a dream is your brain's improvised answer to its own static. Meaning made from noise.
But other researchers think dreams do real work.
While you sleep, the brain replays and reorganises the day, deciding what to keep and what to discard.
The dream may be the visible surface of that maintenance, your mind making sense of you.
That would also explain nightmares.
One strong theory is that dreams are a rehearsal space, a safe simulator where the brain runs through threats and fears.
A nightmare is not a punishment. It is your mind stress-testing you, in a world with no consequences.
Dreams also seem to cool down emotion.
During REM, the brain switches off much of its stress chemistry, letting you revisit difficult experiences calmer.
It is like overnight therapy, taking the sting out of the day, so you wake a little lighter.
And then there is memory.
Study after study shows sleep, and REM in particular, strengthens what you learned and prunes what you did not.
The dream is the soundtrack to that consolidation, your brain deciding which pieces of today become you tomorrow.
So where do dreams come from? From the machine itself.
Random sparks below, a storyteller above, and your own memory and emotion as the raw footage.
A dream is your brain's nightly cinema, remembering, rehearsing, and making sense of you.
As for why you forget them, the recording system simply switches off.
The chemicals that lay down long-term memory are low during REM, so unless you wake mid-dream, the film is never saved.
You are not losing your dreams. They were never written to disk in the first place.
Except sometimes, the watcher wakes up inside the film.
In a lucid dream you realise you are dreaming, and the machine briefly takes direction.
It proves the point beautifully. The whole world you experience is rendered by your own mind, from the inside.
So the next time a dream slips away at breakfast, do not mourn it. It did its job.
It cooled an emotion, filed a memory, rehearsed a fear, and made sense of a day.
The machine was working. You just were not awake to watch the show.
Dreams are not messages from somewhere else. They are the sound of your own mind, maintaining itself in the dark.
And once you see that, sleeping stops being a switch-off, and starts being the most private, creative thing your brain does every night.
